Our journey

How we got here, one question at a time

We built this in stages. Each stage asked one question, tested the answer honestly, and showed what the next stage needed. The tools from every stage are still here to explore.

  1. 1

    A first prototype on real pump data

    Real pump data15–29 July 2026 · 579 wells

    Can routine pump records be turned into water-level forecasts at all?

    We received 15 days of real records: about 490,000 pump readings and 12,355 pumping sessions, each with the water level when the pump started and stopped. We cleaned them, linked readings to sessions, and built models that predict the level at the end of each pump run and at the next start. We then tested those models on the last four days.

    Yes, it worksthe pipeline from raw records to forecasts runs end to end
    ≈ 9 mtypical miss per pump run, because the raw readings are noisy
    35%of sessions had readings too odd to trust, and needed screening out

    Fifteen days could not show seasons or test rainfall: adding rain changed accuracy by just 0.03%. That told us we needed longer histories.

    Open the first prototype
  2. 2

    A test system where we know the answer

    Synthetic test system450 simulated wells · 6 months

    What matters more: better data, or a cleverer model?

    We built a simulated system of 450 wells where the true groundwater level is always known, with deliberately hard cases such as faulty sensors and heavy pumping. Then we compared three approaches on it, each given only the kind of data a real system would have.

    4.2 m → 0.5 merror cut simply by using resting-level readings instead of readings taken while pumping
    → 0.3 mby also using pumping, rainfall and water-supply information
    Sensor driftno model can fix a sensor that slowly drifts: calibration records are essential

    The lesson: better data beats a bigger model. This shaped our request for resting-level readings and continuous logging.

    Three approaches compared The hidden-truth test Scenario explorer
  3. 3

    A full year of monitoring

    Digital twinAug 2025 – Jul 2026 · 579 wells

    How far ahead can we forecast, and how sure can we be?

    A digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the same 579 wells) gave us a full year of data in the company's format: 7.8 million pump readings, 268,000 sessions, and a complete monsoon. We forecast each well's resting level up to 12 weeks ahead and tested every forecast against what followed.

    0.3 mtypical error one week ahead
    ½the error of "nothing changes", 12 weeks ahead
    80%of the time, the real level landed inside our "80% likely" range
    −32%error at 12 weeks from using rainfall
    Try a forecast How accurate What moves the water
  4. 4

    How wells affect each other

    Simulation450 simulated wells · realistic crack network

    Can a model learn which wells' pumping hurts their neighbours?

    We simulated a city whose groundwater flows along cracks in hard rock. We gave our model data like the company's plus an imperfect geology map, and checked what it could recover. We confirmed the results on a second simulated city it had never seen.

    73–80%of the true top-30 pressure-point wells found
    Within 7%of the true strength of the links, with continuous logging
    Not yetexact well-to-well links: that needs a short, minute-by-minute pumping test
    See the simulation
  5. →

    Next: prove it on real wells

    Every long-range result above comes from simulations. The next stage repeats these tests on real long-term records from the company's wells. We are also developing a 7-day early warning for wells about to run dry.

    What we need next
Three lessons that run through every stage
  1. Better data beats a bigger model. The biggest gains came from the right readings (resting levels, continuous logging), not from complexity.
  2. Test as if it were real. Every forecast was made without seeing the future, and checked afterwards. An automatic test proves nothing leaked.
  3. Say how sure you are. Every forecast carries a range, and we check that the range holds as often as it claims.
Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: real pump data (15 days, July 2026), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). Nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
